procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 16, 1963 of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 154 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Magistrate acquitted the accused, but the High Court took the opposite view and convicted the accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant came to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether prejudice was caused to the appellant by the production of a notification for the first time at the appellate stage.

facts: A notification dated January 22, 1955, was introduced for the first time during the appeal in the High Court, not at the original trial.
The appellant claimed that this late introduction of evidence caused them prejudice.
At the trial court, the appellant's argument had been that such a notification was legally insufficient to create a presumption under Section 7 of the Act.
The appellant did not ask the High Court for any additional opportunity to present evidence or arguments to counter the notification.
application: The Supreme Court first noted that the appellant's original argument at trial was not about the existence of the notification, but its legal sufficiency. The Court found this argument was "not tenable."
The Court reasoned that the appellant had "ample opportunity" to rebut the legal presumption that arose under Section 7 of the Act, which was the central issue.

Crucially, the Court pointed out that the appellant never requested more time or a further opportunity from the High Court to address the notification. This failure to ask for a chance to respond indicated that no actual prejudice had occurred.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, holding that no prejudice had been caused because the appellant had sufficient opportunity to rebut the legal presumption and had not requested any further opportunity from the High Court to do so after the notification was produced.

issue.issue_text: Whether the search warrant was invalid as it did not ex-facie set out the authority under which it was issued.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that the search warrant was invalid because it did not, on its face ('ex-facie'), state the authority under which it was issued.
law: The Supreme Court generally does not allow new legal arguments to be raised for the first time at the final appellate stage if they were not presented in the lower courts or in the petition for appeal.
application: The Court noted that this specific argument about the warrant's facial invalidity had not been made in the High Court or in the special leave petition to the Supreme Court.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the point was raised for the first time at this late stage, the Supreme Court refused to allow the argument to be made and did not consider its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant successfully rebutted the presumption under s. 7 that the house was used as a common gaming house.

facts: When police raided the appellant's house, the occupants resisted entry.
Inside, the police found that the occupants had attempted to burn, destroy, and conceal playing cards.
The appellant offered an explanation that he had invited friends and relatives for his son's betrothal.
law: The seizure of instruments of gaming under s. 6 of the Bombay Prevention of Gambling Act raises a presumption under s. 7 that the house was used as a common gaming house.
This presumption can be rebutted if it is apparent there was a reasonable probability that the items (e.g., playing cards) were not being used for gaming or for the profit of the occupier.
application: The Court found that the appellant's actions did not rebut the presumption but instead "fortified" (strengthened) it.
Specifically, the resistance to the police's entry and the attempt to destroy the playing cards were seen as evidence of guilt.
The Court also found the appellant's explanation that the gathering was for his son's betrothal to be "not convincing."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant could not successfully rebut the presumption that his house was being used as a common gaming house because his actions strengthened the presumption of guilt and his explanation was not credible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether prejudice was caused to the appellant by the production of a notification for the first time at the appellate stage.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that prejudice was caused by the production of the notification for the first time at the appellate stage.
The appellant contended in the trial court that such a notification was not sufficient for raising the presumption under s. 7.
respondent_arguments: No prejudice was caused to the appellant, as he had ample opportunity to rebut the presumption arising under s. 7 and did not ask the High Court for any further opportunity to do so.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the search warrant was invalid as it did not ex-facie set out the authority under which it was issued.
appellant_arguments: The search warrant was invalid as it did not ex-facie set out the authority under which it was issued.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument, but the court's reasoning implies a procedural objection that the point was not raised in the lower courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant successfully rebutted the presumption under s. 7 that the house was used as a common gaming house.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the presumption was rebutted, contending that the notification produced was not sufficient to raise the presumption in the first place.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument, but the implied argument is that the appellant failed to rebut the presumption.

cases.principle: An authorization of a person holding a specific office (in that case, the second class magistrate of Thirumangalam) constitutes a special empowering of that person by virtue of their office.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An officer can be specially empowered under a statute either by their personal name or by virtue of their office or official title.
obiter: In applying an artificial statutory presumption, the court should act with circumspection.

The presumption that a house was used as a common gaming house can be rebutted if prosecution evidence itself shows a reasonable probability that items, such as playing cards, were not kept or used as a means of gaming or for the profit of the occupier.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The conviction was upheld because the statutory presumption under s. 7 that the appellant's house was used as a common gaming house was validly raised and the appellant failed to rebut it. The appellant's procedural challenge regarding the late production of a notification was rejected as no prejudice was shown, given he had ample opportunity to rebut the presumption and did not request more time. A separate challenge to the search warrant's validity was procedurally barred as it was not raised in the lower courts.
legal_tests_applied: The presumption under s. 7 that a house was used as a common gaming house can be rebutted if from the prosecution evidence itself it is apparent that there was a reasonable probability of the playing cards not being kept or used as means of gaming or for profit or gain of the occupier of the house.
why_appellant_lost: No prejudice was caused by the late production of the notification because the appellant had ample opportunity to rebut the resulting presumption and did not ask the High Court for any further opportunity to do so.
The court refused to allow the appellant to argue that the search warrant was invalid because the point was not taken either in the High Court or in the special leave petition.
The appellant could not successfully rebut the presumption under s. 7 that the house was used as a common gaming house.
why_respondent_won: The appellant was not prejudiced by the timing of the notification's production, as he had a full opportunity to rebut the presumption it supported.
The appellant's challenge to the search warrant was procedurally barred by the court for not being raised earlier.
The seizure of instruments of gaming raised the statutory presumption under s. 7, and the appellant failed to provide evidence to rebut it.
policy_considerations: In applying the 'artificial presumption' under s. 7, the court should act with circumspection, as playing cards can be kept and used for innocent pastime.
